# Mahāgosiṅga Sutta (MN 32 (PTS MN i 212))
**ID:** MN 32 (PTS MN i 212)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāgosiṅga Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 212
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn32

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāgosiṅga Sutta* (MN 32) is set on a clear moonlit night in the Gosiṅga sāla-tree grove, where several eminent disciples gather [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Sāriputta asks each elder in turn what type of practitioner would illuminate and adorn the forest [SuttaCentral; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The disciples provide answers reflecting distinct spiritual ideals: Ānanda praises the monk who has heard much and can teach all audiences effectively, while Mahāmoggallāna describes two monks engaging in doctrinal discussion (*abhidhammakathā*) who question each other without faltering [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anderson 1999]. When the elders relate their exchange to the Buddha, he endorses all their responses as well spoken, but adds his own ideal: a monastic who enters meditation with the resolute determination not to break posture until all mental defilements are fully eradicated [Anālayo 2017; Buswell & Lopez 2014].
The sutta's mention of *abhidhammakathā* is prominent in Buddhist exegetical and modern scholarship. Buddhaghosa cites the text in his commentary to the *Abhidhamma Piṭaka* as scriptural authority that mastery of Abhidhamma enables monks to resolve doctrinal questions correctly [Anderson 1999; Anderson 2013]. Scholars observe that in this early discourse, *abhidhamma* functions alongside *dhammakathā*, signifying discussion "about" or "concerning" the Dhamma rather than a reference to a finalized Abhidhamma collection [Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma; Klaus & Hartmann 2007].
SuttaCentral identifies full parallels in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 184), the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 37.3), an individual Chinese translation (T 154.16), and a Sanskrit fragment (SHT sutta63) [SuttaCentral]. Significant recensional variations exist: the *Madhyama-āgama* parallel attributes the *abhidharma* discussion to Mahākaccāna (adding the qualifier *gambhīra*, "profound"), whereas three Chinese versions and the Sanskrit fragment instead attribute the exercise of supernormal powers to Mahāmoggallāna [Klaus & Hartmann 2007; Watanabe 1983]. One Chinese parallel lacks any mention of *abhidharma* [Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma]. In DharmaNexus, the sutta shares extensive passages with the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10, AN 5, AN 4, AN 3, AN 6), the *Kassapa Saṁyutta* (SN 16), and the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments by DharmaNexus also match the *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26) and *Ekottarika-āgama* (T 125) (confirming SuttaCentral's curated parallels), along with alignments in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].
